axes.x: Northeast along the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy tracks, toward Gridley Street and Galesburg. Hail Street is x = 0. This direction is 29.8 degrees east of true north.
axes.z: Across the tracks. Positive z in this file is the side drawn with West Main, Dean, Jackson, and Washington. Negative z is the side drawn with East Main, Crafford, Rile, and Sperry. The viewer mirrors this axis, because positive z is geographic east once x points northeast, which had swapped the two Main streets. After the mirror, positive z is east.

tracks.name: C. B. & Q. main line
tracks.notes: The Northern Cross, renamed into the CB&Q, was graded across the town site before the 1854 plat. Streets were laid parallel to it. One main track plus a siding is inferred; the 1886 map shows railroad ground wide enough for more than a single rail.

tracks.name: House track
tracks.notes: A siding serving the depot and the 1880 elevator. The alignment beside the depot is inferred.

tracks.name: T. P. & W.
tracks.notes: Surveyed through Bushnell in 1867. By 1885 the county history calls it part of the Wabash. The Keokuk Junction Railway inherited the route and still crosses the Burlington at about a right angle, parallel to Hail Street, 1,680 feet southwest of the Hail crossing. That is just southwest of Davis Street.

buildings.name: Bushnell House
buildings.notes: A leading hotel by 1885, described as opposite the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy station. Placed on East Main facing the depot grounds. The exact lot is inferred.

buildings.name: Cole Building
buildings.notes: James Cole's brick corner at East Main and Hail. He made the bricks himself in the 1860s. He added banking in 1878. Sourced from the centennial photograph of the original building: two stories, four upstairs windows under segmental arches, a bracketed cornice, pilasters, and a cast-iron storefront with the door at the Hail corner. The early-1900s taller round-arched Cole Block is not drawn. The 48-foot street front is the four-bay width of that photograph; the depth is the ordinary store depth, inferred.

facade.photoDate: 1860s building. The photograph is undated and was printed in 1954. An early-1900s view of a taller round-arched Cole Block was not used.
facade.photoSource: Bushnell, Illinois, centennial, 1854–1954. The photograph is captioned as the original Cole building at East Main and Hail.

buildings.name: Farmers National Bank
buildings.notes: Organized in 1871 from the private bank of Chandler & Cummings, Charles Wilson president. It closed in 1885. Mark places it on the corner of East Main and Hail. The undated East Main postcard titled Bank and Dentist shows a narrow two-story brick front: three upstairs windows under segmental arches, a bracketed cornice, a cast-iron ground floor, and the door on the viewer's right. That front is used here, about 32 feet wide, with the Hail edge kept at the curb. The Farmers and Merchants bank at 484 East Main opened in 1914 and is not drawn.

facade.photoDate: Undated postcard. The seller's title is East Main Street, Bank and Dentist. Farmers and Merchants at 484 East Main opened in 1914, so that later bank is not what is drawn.
facade.photoSource: Mary L. Martin, Bushnell Illinois East Main Street Bank and Dentist Postcard AA60496.

buildings.name: General Store

buildings.name: Clothing

buildings.name: Post Office
buildings.notes: Mark places the post office east along Hail from the Farmers National Bank, on the north side of Hail, with the furniture store beyond it beside the alley. This is the first store east of East Main on that side. The brick front already on the lot is kept. A 2026 school history says that around 1881 a post office building stood on the north side of the first block of East Hurst. Mark's Hail door is the one drawn.

buildings.name: Furniture
buildings.notes: Mark places a furniture store east of the post office on Hail, next to the alley. The narrow gap between this front and the post office is that alley. The brick front already on the lot is kept. He did not name the proprietor. Miller and Krouser's furniture trade, a little east of the Bushnell House, is a different door and is left where it was.

buildings.name: St. Charles Hotel
buildings.notes: The St. Charles was kept by L. H. Green on Hurst Street. The side of Hurst and the lot are inferred.

buildings.name: American House
buildings.notes: The centennial history calls the American House one of Bushnell's first hotels and says the old frame building stood on East Hurst. The lot along East Hurst is inferred.

buildings.name: National Hotel
buildings.notes: Built by the Negleys and later kept by A. Hess on Crafford Street, opposite the East Park. The park block is inferred, and the hotel is placed across Crafford from that block.

buildings.name: Christian Church
buildings.notes: The old Christian Church stood at the corner of Hurst and Dean, later the fire-house corner. Placed on that corner, on the downtown side. Frame construction is inferred.

buildings.name: Presbyterian Church
buildings.notes: A Presbyterian congregation was here by the 1880s, and a later church stands on West Hurst. A centennial photo taken by the Presbyterian Church shows the Christian Church at Hurst and Dean, so the two stood near each other. This lot is inferred.

buildings.name: Methodist Episcopal Church
buildings.notes: Methodist and German Methodist congregations are named in the 1885 biographies. Their buildings are not pinned to a corner in the sources used here, so this church marks the denomination on a residential block east of Crafford.

buildings.name: C. B. & Q. Depot
buildings.notes: The older wooden Chicago, Burlington & Quincy depot, photographed while it was being moved after a newer station was built. Sourced from that photograph: a long single-story clapboard body, a gable with deep bracketed eaves, a three-window bay on the long track side, a door toward each end, a platform, and a brick chimney at one end of the ridge. The model puts that building back in the railroad ground between the two Main streets. The later brick depot is not built. The exact window count is read from a small print, so the spacing is the photograph's rhythm rather than a measured elevation.

buildings.name: Depot Lunch Room
buildings.notes: J. M. Varner & Son kept the depot lunch room. The 1885 history describes the business; the year it opened is not stated, so it is shown as a small frame room by the platform.

buildings.name: Hendee Elevator
buildings.notes: Built in 1880 by S. A. Hendee & Co. Sourced size: 42 by 66 feet, 27,000 bushels. Mark does not know the lot. The centennial says the elevator stood on the railroad ground in front of the Hendee House, and the about-1902 view from that hotel looks at its end. It is placed there, north of the wooden depot and clear of the lunch room. The 1886 Sanborn shows a grain elevator in the railroad ground. The crib, headhouse, cupola, and driveway follow that later photograph. A county-atlas sheet that would pin the footing could not be opened.

facade.photoDate: Built in 1880. The photograph was taken about 1902 from the Alexander Hotel, so the cupola is read from a later picture of the same elevator.
facade.photoSource: Bushnell centennial. The photograph looks southeast from the Alexander Hotel and shows the end of the Hendee elevator across the street.

buildings.name: Freight House
buildings.notes: A freight house beside the depot is the usual CB&Q arrangement and matches the open railroad ground on the 1886 Sanborn. The exact shed is inferred.

buildings.name: Coal & Wood Yard
buildings.notes: Stockton West sold grain, wood, and coal. The yard is placed on the siding. The business is documented; the shed's spot is inferred.

buildings.name: Depot Mill
buildings.notes: The Depot Mill stood by the railroad and was owned by M. H. Hicks. The centennial history places it across from the later Vaughan & Bushnell factory. The footing southwest of the passenger depot is inferred.

buildings.name: Excelsior Mill
buildings.notes: The Excelsior steam flouring mill was built by Nevious Bros. It failed in the fall of 1884 along with the Farmers National Bank, so it was standing in 1880. The centennial history says it stood just west of the Depot Mill. Brick and the smokestack suit a steam mill; the exact corner is inferred.

buildings.name: T. P. & W. Depot
buildings.notes: Mark says this depot still exists and stands on the east side of the tracks. The building still standing is at East Main and Hurst. The McDonough County Voice, 3 February 2016, quoting the Bushnell Historical Society, calls that the only depot left of the town's three, likely built in the mid or late 1800s. The model follows the surviving long gable: cream frame, a row of windows and two doors, a short platform, and a chimney. The 1914 postcard, with a bay and a platform roof on posts, is the station a later caption puts just west of West Main. That bay is not on the building still standing, so it is not drawn here.

facade.photo: The depot still standing at East Main and Hurst

buildings.name: Sorter House
buildings.notes: The Sorter House stood opposite the T. P. & W. station. It stays by the crossing southwest of Davis, on the west side of the Burlington. Mark places the depot that still exists on the east side, at East Main and Hurst, so this hotel is no longer across the street from that building. T. J. Sorter appears among the 1882 charter members of the local Knights of Pythias.

buildings.name: Bushnell Pump Company
buildings.notes: Nelson, LaTourette & Company opened the works in 1872. By 1885 the Bushnell Pump Company occupied a large frame building opposite the old Wabash depot and made wooden pumps, windmills, and croquet sets. It stays beside the crossing southwest of Davis. The depot Mark identifies as the one still standing is on the east side of the tracks at East Main and Hurst.

buildings.name: Roach Livery
buildings.notes: John Roach had kept a livery in Bushnell for about ten years by 1885, so a stable was here around 1880. The history places it at the corner of West Main and First Street. No First Street survives on the plat, so the barn is shown at West Main near Barnes. The big 45-by-80 barn with a 15-by-80 shed was built in 1885, just after this scene, and is drawn a little smaller.

buildings.name: Ball Bros.

facade.photoDate: The 1880s, as captioned. Printed in the 1954 centennial.
facade.photoSource: Bushnell centennial. The photograph is captioned 'The Ball Bros. corner in the 80's at East Main and Gridley Streets.'

buildings.notes: Sourced from the centennial photograph captioned as the Ball Bros. corner in the 1880s, and from the 1885 sizes. The photograph shows a two-story frame shop: light clapboard, one triangular false front across the whole width, BALL BROS. in the gable, three flat-headed upstairs windows, a double door between two shop windows, and a shed porch on posts. This is the East Main front. Mark says the north end, along Gridley, is the two-story brick block that still stands and still looks as it did in 1880. That brick block is the next building. The 1895 60-by-100-foot works is the later enlargement and is not substituted for this corner.

buildings.name: Ball Bros. Gridley block
buildings.notes: Mark says the Gridley building, the oldest one still standing, was two-story brick, and that the north end looks today as it did in 1880. This is that block, red brick, two stories, segmental upstairs windows, and an iron storefront, on the 28-by-48-foot repository size from the 1885 history. The Main Street corner keeps the 1880s false-front photograph. Packard-era pictures of the later works show plate-glass display windows; those later windows are not copied. An open photograph of the present north wall was not found, so the bay spacing is the ordinary twelve-foot brick rhythm.

buildings.name: High School
buildings.notes: Mark places the 1875 high school at Jackson and Cole, not Twyman, and says it had a cupola. It was the high school into the 1930s and the junior high in the 1970s. Jackson and Cole both run parallel to the tracks and do not meet. Cole Street is the next street east of Sperry. The school whose dates match his memory is the East Side School at Cole and Hurst, and an East Side High School postcard shows a two-story brick school with a central door and a cupola. The model stands on that corner, with the stone base and eight classrooms from the 1885 description, and with that cupola. Twyman Street stays. A 2026 school history puts an 1875 building at Jackson and Twyman and says it burned in 1896. That account is recorded. This corner is the one that fits what Mark described.

buildings.name: Reformed Church
buildings.notes: Organized October 19, 1856. Built in 1860 or 1861 at the northwest corner of East Gridley and Crafford, dedicated May 1, 1861. The corner is sourced. No photograph was found, so the white frame walls, front gable, three tall side windows, and modest steeple are the ordinary 1861 form, inferred. The sign is the congregation's name.

buildings.notes: A house facing Gridley Street. A photograph in the 1954 centennial, taken while East and West Main were being paved and captioned as a view west on Gridley from East Main, shows frame houses with porches along this street. That paving was finished in 1904, so the picture is later than 1880. These houses follow that street, not one particular home. No name is attached to this door.

A photograph in the 1954 centennial, taken while East and West Main were being paved and captioned as a view west on Gridley from East Main, shows frame houses with porches along this street. That paving was finished in 1904, so the picture is later than 1880. These houses follow that street, not one particular home. No name is attached to this door.
